prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- The designers behind a "thinking" yacht are hoping to break a world record by sending it across the Atlantic Ocean without any human assistance. The autonomous yacht Avalon is hoisted to have her keel put in place before launching . The four-meter boat, "Avalon", was designed and built by an eight-strong team of third-year engineering students at Swiss science university ETH Zurich. The students are planning to take the boat to a robotic sailing regatta in July, before launching it into the Microtransat Transatlantic challenge in early September. Using sensors to detect the speed and direction of the wind, the boat is programmed to reach a given co-ordinate and will attain it by automatically adapting to the changing conditions. One of the "Students Sailing Autonomously" (SSA) team's project managers, Hendrik Erckens, told CNN that if the Atlantic crossing succeeds it will be a world record as an unmanned boat has not previously made the voyage. It is planned the crossing will begin from the west coast of Ireland and finish in the Caribbean. "For us the Microtransat challenge is the big goal. I'm pretty confident we can do it. This week in testing it is pretty much doing what it's supposed to do. And it is water tight. "Over the last couple of days we tried some autonomous tacks and jibes and now we are testing the navigation," he said. See photos of the autonomous yacht from construction to launch » . The team has been working on the project since September 2008, and are currently at the on-water testing stage, having designed and built the boat. While the team will be able to track the boat through an onboard global positioning system (GPS) during the transatlantic voyage, Erckens said as long as the challenge is active they won't have any control over the vessel. "We will set it out and it will be completely autonomous. There are solar cells on the back for power and extra power supplies on board. "There is a satellite communication system on board and the boat can download weather information by itself so it can calculate the best route to travel," he said. Erckens said the team is positive that the carbon-fibre boat will survive the rough Atlantic seas -- an issue that has stopped many manned crossings before -- including Richard Branson's attempt at the fastest transatlantic crossing aboard the 99-foot Virgin Money last fall. "We feel our advantage over other teams is that we are mechanical engineers. We have designed this boat ourselves and exactly for this purpose." Erckens said the idea could one day offer a new autopilot option for large yachts. "The idea came as there are autopilots for boats out there, but currently the commercially available autopilots only steer the rudder. We are looking to control the sails as well."

The autonomous yacht *Avalon* is hoisted into the air to have its keel installed before launch.

The four-meter vessel was designed and built by a team of eight third-year engineering students at the Swiss science university ETH Zurich. The students plan to enter the boat in a robotic sailing regatta in July before launching it in the Microtransat Transatlantic Challenge in early September.

Using sensors to detect wind speed and direction, the boat is programmed to reach a specified coordinate, automatically adapting to changing conditions along the way.

The crossing is scheduled to begin off the west coast of Ireland and end in the Caribbean.

“For us, the Microtransat Challenge is the big goal. I’m pretty confident we can do it. During testing this week, it has been doing pretty much what it is supposed to do—and it is watertight.

“Over the last couple of days, we have tried several autonomous tacks and jibes, and now we are testing the navigation,” he said.

*See photos of the autonomous yacht, from construction to launch »*

The team has been working on the project since September 2008. Having designed and built the boat, its members are now conducting on-water tests.

Although the team will be able to track the boat through an onboard global positioning system (GPS) during the transatlantic voyage, Erckens said they will have no control over the vessel while the challenge is underway.

“We will set it out, and it will be completely autonomous. There are solar cells on the back to provide power, as well as additional power supplies onboard.

“There is also a satellite communication system onboard, and the boat can download weather information by itself, allowing it to calculate the best route,” he said.

Erckens said the team is confident that the carbon-fiber boat will survive the rough Atlantic seas—conditions that have thwarted many previous crewed crossings, including Richard Branson’s attempt last fall to make the fastest transatlantic crossing aboard the 99-foot *Virgin Money*.

“We feel our advantage over other teams is that we are mechanical engineers. We designed this boat ourselves, specifically for this purpose.”

Erckens said the concept could one day offer a new autopilot option for large yachts.

“The idea arose because autopilots for boats already exist, but the commercially available systems currently control only the rudder. We are looking to control the sails as well.”

LONDON, England (CNN) — The team that created an intelligent, self-navigating yacht hopes to establish a world record by completing an Atlantic crossing with no human intervention.

Before launch, the autonomous vessel, Avalon, was lifted so its keel could be installed. The four-meter yacht was developed and constructed by a group of eight third-year engineering students from ETH Zurich, a Swiss science university.

The students intend to enter Avalon in a robotic sailing regatta in July. In early September, they plan to send it on the Microtransat Transatlantic Challenge.

Equipped with sensors that measure wind direction and speed, the boat is programmed to travel to a specified coordinate. It responds automatically to changing weather and sailing conditions to reach its destination.

Hendrik Erckens, one of the project managers for the “Students Sailing Autonomously” (SSA) team, told CNN that a successful Atlantic voyage would set a world record because no unmanned boat has completed the crossing before.

The planned route starts on Ireland’s west coast and ends in the Caribbean.

“The Microtransat Challenge is our main objective,” Erckens said. “I’m quite confident that we can succeed. During tests this week, the boat has largely performed as intended, and it is watertight.

“In the past few days, we have carried out autonomous tacks and jibes, and we are now testing its navigation system.”

Photos document the autonomous yacht’s progress from construction through launch.

The team began the project in September 2008. Having completed the design and construction phases, the students are now testing Avalon on the water.

During the Atlantic voyage, the group will be able to monitor the yacht through its onboard global positioning system (GPS). However, Erckens said that while the challenge is underway, the team will have no ability to control the vessel.

“We will release it, and from then on it will operate entirely on its own,” he said. “Solar panels at the rear will provide energy, and there are additional power supplies aboard.

“The boat also carries a satellite communications system. It can independently download weather data and use that information to work out the best route.”

Erckens said the team believes the carbon-fiber yacht can withstand the Atlantic’s severe conditions. Rough seas have previously defeated numerous crewed attempts, including Richard Branson’s effort the previous fall to achieve the fastest transatlantic crossing aboard the 99-foot Virgin Money.

“We believe our background gives us an advantage over other teams because we are mechanical engineers,” Erckens said. “We designed the boat ourselves specifically for this task.”

He added that the technology might eventually provide a new form of autopilot for large yachts.

“The concept arose because boat autopilots already exist, but the commercial systems currently available control only the rudder,” he said. “Our aim is to operate the sails too.”

A team of engineering students at ETH Zurich has developed Avalon, a four-meter-long autonomous sailing yacht designed to cross the Atlantic Ocean without anyone on board. The vessel is intended to sail from Ireland to the Caribbean using only wind power for propulsion, while its electronic systems are supplied by solar panels. If successful, Avalon would complete what the team hopes will be the first unmanned Atlantic crossing by a sailing boat and establish a new world record.

Avalon relies on a combination of wind sensors, GPS receivers, onboard computers, and automated steering and sail-control systems. The wind sensors measure the speed and direction of the wind, while GPS data allows the yacht to determine its location and follow a planned route. Its navigation software can then adjust the rudder and sails to respond to changing weather and sea conditions.

Because the yacht must operate for weeks without direct human assistance, the system has been designed to make decisions independently. Avalon can alter its heading, avoid inefficient courses, and carry out essential sailing maneuvers such as tacking and jibing. Its adaptive navigation system is also intended to account for shifts in wind direction and other conditions that could push the boat away from its intended path.

Solar panels provide power for the sensors, computers, communication equipment, and mechanical controls. The yacht must carefully manage this limited energy supply throughout the voyage, particularly during periods of poor weather or reduced sunlight. Its compact structure and watertight construction are equally important, as even a small leak or mechanical failure could threaten the mission far from land.

During early trials, Avalon demonstrated that it could navigate autonomously, tack, jibe, and maintain control without a crew. Tests also indicated that the hull remained watertight, providing confidence that the vessel could withstand prolonged exposure to open-ocean conditions.

The Atlantic crossing will nevertheless present far greater challenges than coastal testing. Avalon will need to cope with strong winds, high waves, changing currents, storms, and possible equipment failures while remaining on course. The project therefore represents not only an attempt at a record but also an experiment in autonomous marine engineering. A successful voyage could help advance technologies for unmanned research vessels, environmental monitoring, and other long-duration ocean missions.

# Swiss students set sights on unmanned Atlantic crossing with autonomous yacht

**Zurich, Switzerland** — A team of engineering students at ETH Zurich is preparing to send an autonomous sailing yacht across the Atlantic Ocean — without a crew and with no one steering from shore.

The vessel, named **Avalon**, was developed for the **Microtransat Challenge**, an international competition aimed at achieving a fully autonomous transatlantic crossing by a small robotic boat.

Once launched, Avalon will have to navigate changing winds, powerful currents, storms and busy shipping routes using onboard computers, sensors and satellite positioning. Unlike a remotely operated vessel, the yacht is designed to make its own decisions at sea, including how to adjust its sails and remain on course.

The project combines naval architecture, mechanical engineering, electronics and artificial intelligence. Because communication across the ocean can be slow or unreliable, the yacht must be able to detect problems and respond without waiting for instructions from its creators.

That makes reliability one of the team’s biggest challenges. Saltwater corrosion, heavy waves and constant mechanical movement can damage equipment over a voyage expected to last several weeks. Even a minor failure — such as a jammed rudder or malfunctioning sail control — could end the attempt.

Avalon’s designers have sought to keep the vessel compact and energy efficient. Solar panels provide power for navigation systems, communications equipment and the actuators that control the boat, while the wind supplies its propulsion.

The yacht will transmit limited data to the team during the crossing, allowing students to monitor its position and condition. But under the challenge’s rules, human operators cannot guide it around bad weather or take control of its steering.

The Microtransat Challenge has attracted university teams, researchers and independent engineers seeking to push the limits of autonomous marine technology. The Atlantic has proved a formidable test: Robotic boats must survive long periods beyond direct human assistance while coping with conditions that can overwhelm much larger vessels.

For the ETH Zurich students, Avalon is more than a race entry. Technologies tested aboard autonomous sailboats could eventually be used for oceanographic research, environmental monitoring and maritime surveillance, allowing low-energy vessels to spend months collecting data at sea.

If Avalon completes the journey, it would mark a major engineering achievement for the student team — and offer a glimpse of a future in which some of the world’s oceans are explored not by crews, but by machines capable of sailing on their own.

# Swiss students design carbon-fibre yacht to cross the Atlantic without a crew

**Eight third-year students at ETH Zurich have developed an autonomous sailing boat intended to navigate from Ireland to the Caribbean without human assistance.**

**Zurich, Switzerland —** Crossing the Atlantic in a small yacht is a demanding test of seamanship. Doing it without anyone on board requires a different kind of sailor: one made from sensors, software and electronics.

A team of eight undergraduate students at ETH Zurich has designed a lightweight carbon-fibre yacht capable of steering itself across the ocean, adjusting its sails and responding to changing wind and weather conditions along the way.

The proposed route would take the vessel from Ireland to the Caribbean, relying primarily on wind for propulsion and onboard renewable energy to power its computers, communications equipment and control systems.

Unlike remotely piloted boats, the yacht is intended to make most navigational decisions independently. Data from instruments monitoring wind, position and the boat’s movement would be fed into an onboard computer, which would determine its course and operate the rudder and sails.

That autonomy is essential in the middle of the Atlantic, where communications can be slow or unreliable. Although the vessel could transmit status updates and receive high-level instructions, it would not depend on a person continuously controlling it from shore.

### Building for an unforgiving ocean

The students chose carbon fibre to create a hull that is both light and strong. Reducing weight allows the yacht to move more efficiently in weak winds, while the material’s rigidity helps it withstand repeated exposure to waves and changing loads.

But an unmanned crossing presents challenges beyond keeping the boat afloat.

Every critical system must continue working for weeks at sea, despite salt water, strong winds and constant motion. Components also need backups or fail-safe settings because there will be no crew available to carry out repairs.

The yacht’s software must cope with conditions that cannot be perfectly predicted before departure. That includes avoiding dangerous weather, staying on course when winds shift and conserving electrical power during periods of limited sunlight.

The students have had to combine naval architecture, mechanical engineering, electronics and computer science — fields that are usually handled by separate specialist teams in commercial marine projects.

### A floating robotics laboratory

Autonomous vessels are attracting growing interest from researchers and the maritime industry. Crewless boats could eventually be used to collect climate data, inspect offshore infrastructure or monitor remote stretches of ocean at a lower cost than conventional research ships.

Sail-powered platforms offer an additional advantage: Their main source of propulsion does not require fuel. That could allow them to remain at sea for long periods while producing fewer emissions.

For the ETH Zurich team, however, the Atlantic route is first and foremost an engineering benchmark. A successful crossing would demonstrate that a relatively small student-built vessel can operate reliably over thousands of kilometers with little or no intervention.

Before attempting the full journey, the yacht would need to complete extensive trials in controlled waters, with the team testing its steering, sail controls, communications and emergency procedures.

The ocean will provide the final examination — and unlike a university test, it will not offer partial credit.
